**Illustrations**
(a) A lays sticks and turf over a pit, with the intention of thereby causing death, or with the knowledge that death is likely to be thereby caused. Z believing the ground to be firm, treads on it, falls in and is killed. A has committed the offence of culpable homicide.
(b) A knows Z to be behind a bush. B does not know it. A, intending to cause, or knowing it to be likely to cause Z's death, induces B to fire at the bush. B fires and kills Z. Here B may be guilty of no offence; but A has committed the offence of culpable homicide.
(c) A, by shooting at a fowl with intent to kill and steal it, kills B who is behind a bush; A not knowing that he was there. Here, although A was doing an unlawful act, he was not guilty of culpable homicide, as he did not intend to kill B, or to cause death by doing an act that he knew was likely to cause death.

**Explanation 1:** A person who causes bodily injury to another who is labouring under a disorder, disease or bodily infirmity, and thereby accelerates the death of that other, shall be deemed to have caused his death.

**Explanation 2:** Where death is caused by bodily injury, the person who causes such bodily injury shall be deemed to have caused the death, although by resorting to proper remedies and skilful treatment the death might have been prevented.

**Explanation 3:** The causing of the death of child in the mother's womb is not homicide. But it may amount to culpable homicide to cause the death of a living child, if any part of that child has been brought forth, though the child may not have breathed or been completely born.

The right of private defence is a fundamental right that allows individuals to protect themselves and others from imminent harm or unlawful aggression when state aid cannot be obtained in time.

### General Principle

-   **Section 96 of the IPC (now Section 34 of the BNS)** states that nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence.

### Scope of the Right of Private Defence of the Body

-   **Section 97 of the IPC (now Section 35 of the BNS)** grants every person the right to defend:

पूर्ण झाल्या असतील आणि कोणत्याही कार्यवाहीत, मूळची पुढील पुरावा किंवा निर्मिती न करता, मूळच्या कोणत्याही सामग्रीचा किंवा

(c) उक्त कालावधीच्या महत्त्वपूर्ण भागामध्ये, संगणक योग्यरित्या कार्यरत होता किंवा, तसे नसल्यास, ज्या कालावधीत तो योग्यरित्या कार्यरत नव्हता किंवा त्या कालावधीच्या त्या भागामध्ये तो कार्यान्वित नव्हता, तो इलेक्ट्रॉनिक रेकॉर्ड किंवा त्याच्या सामग्रीच्या अचूकतेवर परिणाम करणारा नव्हता; आणि
(d) इलेक्ट्रॉनिक रेकॉर्डमध्ये असलेली माहिती उक्त गतिविधींच्या सामान्य क्रमाने संगणकात फीड केलेल्या माहितीची पुनरावृत्ती करते किंवा त्यातून प्राप्त झाली आहे.

(4) कोणत्याही कार्यवाहीत जिथे या कलमाच्या आधारे पुरावा म्हणून विधान देण्याची इच्छा असेल, तिथे खालीलपैकी कोणतीही गोष्ट करणारे प्रमाणपत्र, म्हणजे:

(c) उप-कलम (2) मध्ये नमूद केलेल्या अटींशी व्यवहार करणे,
आणि संबंधित उपकरणाच्या कार्यान्वयनाशी किंवा संबंधित गतिविधींच्या व्यवस्थापनाशी संबंधित जबाबदार अधिकृत पदावर असलेल्या व्यक्तीने (जे योग्य असेल ते) स्वाक्षरी केलेले असल्याचे भासवणारे प्रमाणपत्र, प्रमाणपत्रात नमूद केलेल्या कोणत्याही बाबीचा पुरावा असेल; आणि या उप-कलमाच्या उद्देशांसाठी, ती बाब नमूद करणाऱ्या व्यक्तीच्या सर्वोत्तम ज्ञान आणि विश्वासानुसार नमूद करणे पुरेसे असेल.

(5) या कलमाच्या उद्देशांसाठी,
(a) माहिती संगणकाला पुरवली गेली असे मानले जाईल जर ती कोणत्याही योग्य स्वरूपात पुरवली गेली असेल आणि ती थेट पुरवली गेली असेल किंवा (मानवी हस्तक्षेपासह किंवा त्याशिवाय) कोणत्याही योग्य उपकरणाद्वारे;
(b) कोणत्याही अधिकाऱ्याद्वारे चालवल्या जाणाऱ्या गतिविधींच्या दरम्यान, माहिती त्या गतिविधींच्या उद्देशांसाठी संगणकाद्वारे साठवण्यासाठी किंवा प्रक्रिया करण्यासाठी पुरवली जात असेल जी त्या गतिविधींच्या क्रमाने चालवली जात नसेल, तर ती माहिती, जर त्या संगणकाला योग्यरित्या पुरवली गेली असेल, तर ती त्या गतिविधींच्या क्रमाने पुरवली गेली असे मानले जाईल;
(c) संगणक आउटपुट संगणकाद्वारे तयार केले गेले असे मानले जाईल, मग ते थेट तयार केले गेले असेल किंवा (मानवी हस्तक्षेपासह किंवा त्याशिवाय) कोणत्याही योग्य उपकरणाद्वारे.
स्पष्टीकरण: या कलमाच्या उद्देशांसाठी, इतर माहितीमधून माहिती प्राप्त होण्याचा कोणताही संदर्भ गणना, तुलना किंवा इतर कोणत्याही प्रक्रियेद्वारे त्यातून प्राप्त होण्याचा संदर्भ असेल.

respectively. The procedure outlined below incorporates both the old and new legal frameworks.

### I. Registration of First Information Report (FIR)

Upon receiving information relating to the commission of a cognizable offense, the officer in charge of a police station is mandated to record the substance of such information. A copy of the FIR must be given forthwith, free of cost, to the informant. This is provided under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which is now mirrored in Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.

### II. Investigation by Police

Upon registration of an FIR, the police commence investigation into the cognizable offense.

-   **Power to Investigate:** The police officer in charge of a police station is empowered to investigate any cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate. This power is conferred by Section 156 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and Section 175 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.
-   **Procedure of Investigation:** The officer in charge of a police station, on receiving information or otherwise, having reason to suspect the commission of a cognizable offense, shall proceed in person or depute one of his subordinate officers to the spot to investigate the facts and circumstances of the case and, if necessary, to take measures for the discovery and arrest of the offender. This is outlined in Section 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
-   **Examination of Witnesses:** During the investigation, the police officer may examine any person acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case. The statements of such persons are recorded under Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and Section 181 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. These statements are not signed by the person making them.
-   **Recording of Statements and Confessions:** Any statement or confession made in the course of investigation may be recorded by a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and Section 184 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Such statements or confessions must be recorded in the manner provided by the said Section.
-   **Search and Seizure:** The investigating officer may conduct searches for the purpose of discovering any fact relevant to the investigation and seize any property or document that may be material to the case, under Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and Section 185 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.
-   **Medical Examination:** In cases involving physical injury, the victim may be subjected to a medical examination as per Section 164A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and Section 184A of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.

If, during the investigation, the police find sufficient evidence against the accused, they may proceed to arrest the person.

-   **General Provisions for Arrest:** Sections 41 to 60A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and Section 35 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, deal with the provisions relating to arrest. A police officer may arrest any person without a warrant in a cognizable offense.
-   **Notice of Appearance:** In cases where the offense is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may be less
than seven years, the police officer shall issue a notice of appearance to the person against whom a reasonable
complaint has been made, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists that he has
committed a cognizable offense, under Section 41A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, or Section 35(1)(b) of the
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. The person to whom such notice is issued is bound to appear as required in the
notice. The Supreme Court in *Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar, (2014) 8 SCC 273* ([Judgment
PDF](https://api.sci.gov.in/supremecourt/2014/19532/19532_2014_Judgement_02-Jul-2014.pdf)) emphasised that police
officers must not mechanically arrest an accused, especially in cases under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860,
and Magistrates must not authorise detention casually.

Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, stipulate that, save in exceptional circumstances, no woman shall be arrested after
sunset and before sunrise. Where such exceptional circumstances exist, the woman police officer shall, by making a
written report, obtain the prior permission of the Judicial Magistrate of the first class within whose local
jurisdiction the offense is committed or the arrest is to be made.

### IV. Bail

After arrest, the accused may seek bail.

-   **Bailable Offences:** In bailable offenses, the accused has a right to be released on bail, either by the police officer in charge of the station or by the court, upon furnishing a bail bond with or without sureties, under Section 436 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
-   **Non-Bailable Offences:** In non-bailable offenses, bail is not a matter of right but is granted at the discretion
of the court. The court considers various factors such as the nature and gravity of the offense, the severity of the
punishment, the character of the evidence, the apprehension of the accused fleeing from justice, and the possibility of
tampering with witnesses, while deciding on a bail application under Section 437 of the Code of Criminal Procedure,
1973, and Section 480 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.
-   **Anticipatory Bail:** A person apprehending arrest on an accusation of having committed a non-bailable offense may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction that in the event of such arrest, he shall be released on bail, under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and Section 483 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.

### V. Filing of Police Report (Charge Sheet/Final Report)

Upon completion of the investigation, the police officer submits a report to the Magistrate.

-   **Police Report:** As soon as the investigation is completed, the officer in charge of the police station shall
forward to a Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of the offense on a police report, a report in the form prescribed
by the State Government, stating the names of the parties, the nature of the information, the names of the persons who

After the police report is filed, the Magistrate takes cognizance of the offense under Section 190 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and Section 208 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. The Magistrate may also take cognizance upon a complaint made by the victim or upon information received from any person other than a police officer.

-   **Prosecution Evidence:** The prosecution presents its evidence, including examining witnesses and producing documents.

-   **Statement of Accused:** The accused is given an opportunity to explain the circumstances appearing in the evidence against him under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and Section 350 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.
-   **Defense Evidence:** The accused may then present their defense evidence, if any.
-   **Arguments:** Both the prosecution and defense present their final arguments.
-   **Judgment:** The court delivers its judgment, either acquitting or convicting the accused.

## Common Intention

Common intention is a rule of evidence or a principle of constructive liability, not a substantive offence in itself. It is dealt with under Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and its equivalent is Section 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

**Provision:**
Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, states: "When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone."
Similarly, Section 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, provides: "When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone."

**Essentials of Common Intention:**
-   **Several Persons:** There must be two or more persons involved in the commission of the criminal act.
-   **Common Intention:** A "prior meeting of minds" or a pre-arranged plan must exist among the participants. This common intention may be formed before the incident or may develop on the spur of the moment.
-   **Criminal Act:** A criminal act must be committed by one or more of these persons.
-   **In Furtherance:** The criminal act must be done in furtherance of the common intention of all.
-   **Participation:** All individuals must participate in the criminal act, either actively or passively. Mere presence at the scene of the crime is generally not sufficient to establish common intention.

**Liability:**
Under this doctrine, each person is held equally liable for the criminal act as if they had committed it individually.

## Criminal Conspiracy

Criminal conspiracy is a substantive offence under Indian criminal law. It is defined under Section 120A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, with punishment provided in Section 120B. In the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, both the definition and punishment for criminal conspiracy are consolidated under Section 61.

**Provision:**
Section 120A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, defines criminal conspiracy as: "When two or more persons agree to do, or cause to be done,— (1) an illegal act, or (2) an act which is not illegal by illegal means, such an agreement is designated a criminal conspiracy: Provided that no agreement except an agreement to commit an offence shall amount to a criminal conspiracy unless some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties to such agreement in pursuance thereof."

Section 61(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, similarly states: "When two or more persons agree to do, or cause to be done— (a) an illegal act; or (b) an act which is not illegal by illegal means, such an agreement is designated a criminal conspiracy: Provided that no agreement except an agreement to commit an offence shall amount to a criminal conspiracy unless some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties to such agreement in pursuance thereof."

**Essentials of Criminal Conspiracy:**
-   **Two or More Persons:** There must be an agreement between two or more persons.
-   **Agreement:** The essence of the offence lies in the agreement itself, which can be express or implied. The offence is complete the moment the agreement is made.
-   **Object of Agreement:** The agreement must be to commit an illegal act, or a legal act by illegal means.

### New Elements in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 Homicide Provisions

-   **Section 103 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Punishment for murder)**:
-   **New Element**: Sub-section (2) is a completely new addition. It introduces enhanced punishment for "group murder"
where a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on grounds of race, caste, community, sex, place

murder did not exist in Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

-   **Section 106 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Causing death by negligence)**:
    -   **New Element**: This section significantly revises and enhances the provisions for causing death by negligence, which was covered under Section 304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
        -   **Increased General Punishment**: For causing death by rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, the punishment is increased to imprisonment up to five years and fine, compared to up to two years or fine or both under IPC Section 304A.

The punishment for this is imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years and fine. This particular offense and its enhanced punishment were not explicitly covered under IPC Section 304A.
